verses.text: We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.
For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment,
how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,
and was affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.
For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking.
But somewhere it is testified in these words: "What is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?
You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor
and placed everything under his feet." When God subjected all things to him, He left nothing outside of his control. Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.
But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone.
In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering.
For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.
He says: "I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly."
And again: "I will put My trust in Him." And once again: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me."
Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.
For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham.
For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people.
Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.

context.author: Unknown. The letter does not name its author. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, and others have been suggested.
context.genre: A sermon in letter form, rich with Old Testament quotations
context.audience: Jewish Christians tempted to go back to old patterns under pressure
context.setting: After the first warning, the writer explains why the Son took on flesh and blood: to taste death for everyone, to break the power of the one who has the power of death, and to become a merciful and faithful high priest. The Son who is above the angels became lower than them for a little while.
context.custom: The word translated "author" of their salvation (2:10) can also mean pioneer or trailblazer: someone who goes ahead and leads others after him. Being held in slavery by the fear of death (2:15) was a heavy burden in the ancient world.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 3 shows that Jesus is also greater than Moses.
context.timelineBible: Psalm 8:4-6 is read as the destiny of humanity fulfilled in Jesus. Isaiah 8:17-18 gives the picture of the Son with his children.
context.sparkNotes: We must pay closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift. How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? God has put the world to come not under angels but under humanity. We do not yet see everything in subjection, but we see Jesus, crowned with glory because of the suffering of death. Since the children share in flesh and blood, he partook of the same things so that through death he might destroy the devil. He had to be made like his brothers in every respect to be a merciful and faithful high priest.

translation.meaning: A pioneer or leader who goes first.
To make atonement, or to remove wrath and sin.

otBackground.note: “What is man that you are mindful of him?”
Quoted in 2:13: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me."
The seed of the woman will crush the serpent.

overview.summary: The first warning: do not neglect so great a salvation. Jesus became human, suffered, and defeated death, so he can help those who are tempted.
overview.settingLine: Written to Jewish believers under pressure.

history.t: Writers of the time, such as the Epicurean poet Lucretius, argued at length against the fear of death, which suggests how common it was. Hebrews 2:15 says that Jesus frees those who were held in slavery by this fear.
Verse 17 is the first time the letter calls Jesus a high priest. He became "merciful and faithful" by sharing flesh and blood and by being tempted, so he can help those who are tempted (2:18).

customs.t: The verb in 2:1 pictures something slipping past unnoticed, like a boat that drifts by the harbor because no one is paying attention.
The word in 2:10 (archēgos) can mean founder, leader or pioneer: someone who goes ahead and opens the way for others. It returns in 12:2.

archaeology.t: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied about 125 BC, contains Isaiah 8:17-18, the words Hebrews 2:13 quotes: "I will put My trust in Him" and "Here am I, and the children God has given Me."
Papyrus 46, about AD 200, is the oldest large copy of Hebrews. In it the letter stands right after Romans, among the letters of Paul.

overview.discussion: The writer says Jesus was tested and can help those who are tempted. How does it change my prayers to know he knows what temptation feels like?
overview.book: The letter to the Hebrews · 13 chapters. A polished sermon showing that Jesus fulfills and surpasses the old covenant.
overview.author: Unknown

historicalImage.caption: Papyrus 46, usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews, and so it carries chapter 2, where the Son is made like his brothers in every way (2:17). The manuscript is a book of leaves, a codex, and not a roll.

currentImage.caption: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, built over the place that Christian tradition since the 4th century has marked as the site of the crucifixion and the tomb. Hebrews 2:9 says Jesus tasted death for everyone.
